summary.text: 子 is a whole-graph pictograph interpreted as an infant. The child sense fits that image; its use for the first earthly branch has a separate, disputed history.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts an infant as a whole, rather than combining separate components. Shang forms are interpreted as showing a large head, moving arms, and undeveloped or bundled legs; accounts differ on anatomical details.

history.text: The selected seal-script form is a modern redraw of a later reference shape, distinct from the Shang forms described in paleographic accounts. It illustrates a later style but does not document the original pictograph or establish a sequence of graphic changes.

One account describes a more elaborate Shang graph, 𢀈, used for the first earthly branch, and says 子 gradually took its place after the beginning of Zhou. It also describes 子 as used for a child and for the sixth branch, later written 巳. A competing proposal identifies 甾 as the earlier first-branch graph; the sequence remains disputed.
The Han-era lexicographic explanation associates 子 with the eleventh month and the growth of things. This later seasonal interpretation does not identify the graph’s original Shang meaning.

子 was also used loanwise for 慈 and 孜 in Western Zhou inscriptions: the graph was reused to write other words, rather than those words developing from the infant meaning. The available account gives no sound comparison to explain the borrowing.

uncertainties.text: Accounts support interpreting 子 as an infant pictograph but differ over the depicted anatomy. The exact date of the earliest child-use inscription is unresolved; the Shang example and its reading are reported through a secondary account.

The earlier graph for the first earthly branch and the timing or mechanism of branch reassignment are unresolved: accounts propose either 𢀈 or 甾 before 子. The readings do not establish whether the child and branch uses are connected by borrowing.

Reported uses include a clan leader, a person suffix in Warring States Chu slips, and “young/immature.” The chronology connecting these uses with “infant,” and any path to “offspring,” “seed,” or “fruit,” remain unresolved.

senses.period: Shang; exact earliest token date unresolved
senses.text: A paleographic account identifies “infant” as the graph’s original sense and reports a Shang pregnancy-related use in 有子. This is the earliest supported sense here; the exact reading and calendar date of that example remain unresolved.
子 is reported as used for a child in Shang contexts. This fits the infant interpretation, though the evidence does not establish a precise date or a separate transition from “infant.”

子 is attested as the first earthly branch, but the identity of the graph used earlier and the reassignment sequence are disputed. One account places 𢀈 before 子; another proposal identifies 甾. Its relationship to the infant sense is unresolved.
A Shang use for a same-surname clan leader is reported. How it developed from or relates to “infant” is unresolved.
In 君子, 子 is reported as a suffix referring to a person. A semantic path from the child sense to this use is not established.
A later use meaning “young” or “immature” is reported, as in 子薑. Its date and development from the child sense are unresolved.
“Offspring” is a supplied dictionary gloss; its chronology and connection to the earliest infant sense are not documented here.
“Seed” and “fruit” are supplied glosses; their history and development from “infant” or “child” are unresolved.

developments.text: The reported child use is closely related to “infant,” but a dated transition between the two is not documented.

limitations.text: The reported uses do not establish a full chronology or semantic chain among infant, child, clan leader, person suffix, young, offspring, seed, and fruit. The branch use has a separately disputed graphic history.

overview.text: 子 is a whole-graph picture interpreted as an infant, and “child” is an early supported use. Its use for the first earthly branch has a separate, disputed history.
